items.title: The Triffin dilemma haunts reserve currencies
items.claim: Robert Triffin's 1959-60 testimony to the US Congress identified a problem with the Bretton Woods system. What was it?

options.text: The reserve currency issuer (US) had to run current account deficits to supply the world with reserves, but doing so eroded confidence in the currency's gold convertibility — creating a contradiction that would eventually undermine the system
There was nothing to worry about

items.reveal_title: Conflict between domestic and international roles
items.reveal:
Triffin published 'Gold and the Dollar Crisis' (1960) elaborating the argument. The Bretton Woods system collapsed in 1971 when Nixon ended dollar-gold convertibility — exactly as Triffin had predicted.

The dilemma persists in modern form: the dollar's global role still requires the US to provide dollar liquidity (via deficits or swap lines), which raises long-run sustainability questions. China's BRICS-related discussions of reserve diversification are a contemporary echo.
items.why: International monetary architecture has structural tensions that don't disappear because the immediate crisis has passed. Triffin remains relevant 60 years on.

items.title: The UK's 2010-2015 austerity programme
items.claim: The UK government under Osborne (2010-2016) pursued fiscal consolidation. What was the actual deficit reduction trajectory?

options.text: Budget deficit fell from ~10% of GDP (2009-10) to ~4% by 2015-16, but the target of eliminating it by 2015 was missed; growth was slower than OBR projections; public investment was cut sharply

items.reveal:
ONS data: UK fiscal deficit was 10.1% of GDP in 2009-10, 4.1% by 2015-16. The original 2010 emergency budget aimed to balance the structural deficit by 2015; the target was slipped repeatedly.

IFS and OBR analyses found growth fell short of pre-austerity forecasts. Economic historians (Blyth 'Austerity', 2013) and IMF research raised doubts about the timing of consolidation; defenders (Niemietz, others) argued the policy preserved fiscal credibility.

The austerity debate continues; the empirical record is contested but the speed of recovery was slower than baseline.
items.why: Major macroeconomic policy choices have decade-long effects that are hard to evaluate cleanly because counterfactuals are unobservable.

items.title: Potential GDP is not directly observable
items.claim: The output gap is actual GDP minus potential GDP, expressed as a percentage of potential. Why is this concept difficult to use in practice?

options.text: Potential GDP is unobservable — it must be estimated, and estimates are revised heavily after the fact. Pre-2008 estimates of potential GDP have been revised down substantially, suggesting the economy was less overheated than thought
It is observable directly from satellite

items.reveal_title: A concept whose measurement is treacherous
items.reveal:
OECD, IMF and central bank estimates of potential GDP use filters (Hodrick-Prescott, Kalman) and production function approaches. They produce different numbers and revise heavily as data arrives.

Orphanides's 2003 paper showed that real-time output gap estimates available to the Fed in the 1970s were systematically wrong, contributing to policy errors.

The BIS has criticised reliance on output gaps for monetary policy.
items.why: Policy variables that depend on unobservable concepts inherit estimation uncertainty. Output gap-based 'rules' look cleaner in textbooks than in practice.
